text:
Gus asked his robot, Sprocket, to write up their science experiment as a report. Sprocket wrote a diary.

8:00 am. Gus says today we are finding out which melts ice fastest: salt, sugar or sand. Gus has given me a lab coat. It is too big. I am excited. I have never melted anything before, except a crayon, by accident.

8:15 am. We put three ice cubes of the same size on three plates. Gus sprinkled one spoon of salt on the first, one spoon of sugar on the second and one spoon of sand on the third. Gus says the plates must match and the room must stay the same temperature, or it isn't a fair test.

9:15 am. Results! The salty cube melted completely in 31 minutes. The sugary cube took 48 minutes. The sandy cube took 52 minutes, barely faster than a plain one. I timed them all with my internal clock, which is extremely accurate.

9:20 am. Conclusion: salt melts ice fastest. This is why people put salt on icy roads. Gus says I may write the next report too. I am honoured. He also says I should try pepper next time. I say pepper is for soup.

frame: Indi wrote the chairlift rules for the Scaffold Peaks ski school. The Topsittle rode the chairlift to read them.
text:
The Scaffold Peaks ski school asked Indi to write the chairlift rules for its youngest skiers. She wrote a fairy tale.

Once upon a time, a small skier named Pip came to the chairlift. A wise old wombat was waiting by the gate. 'Before you ride the magic chair,' said the wombat, 'you must learn three secrets.' The first secret was to wait behind the red line until the chair swung round behind you. The second was to sit right back and pull the safety bar down, snug across your tummy. The third, and most important, was never to wriggle, bounce or lean over to look at your boots, no matter how interesting they were. Pip learnt all three secrets. Up and up she floated, past the snow gums and the rock towers, until she reached the top. There she lifted the bar, stood up and skied away, as safe and happy as anyone had ever been. And every child who learns the wombat's secrets rides the magic chair safely, ever after.

The ski school has printed the story on a big sign beside the chairlift, with a picture of the wombat. Since then, not one small skier has wriggled.

answerWith: the text of the one correct option
options: To give older skiers something fun to read while they wait in the queue.
To teach young skiers about the wise wombats that live near the lift.
Because the ski school asked her to write a story for its new sign.
To make the rules easy for very young skiers to follow and remember.

frame: Year 6 is writing to the Minister for the Environment. The Dappella has never seen the class so serious.
text: For a whole term, Year 6 at Scaffold Peaks Primary has been studying Pebble Bay, the small cove at the foot of the island. They have counted the fish in its rock pools, photographed the seals that sunbake on its ledges and collected more than four thousand pieces of plastic from its sand. Their research shows that the bay is home to at least eleven kinds of fish found almost nowhere else, but that boats and rubbish are slowly damaging it. The class has decided to write to the Minister for the Environment, who has the power to turn the bay into a marine sanctuary. The Minister receives hundreds of letters every week and does not know anyone at the school. Ms Ford has warned the class that only letters that are respectful, serious and clearly written will be read past the first line. The class has also collected three hundred signatures from around the island. Wren has been chosen to write that first line, the one that asks for the sanctuary. frame: Wren's little cousin is coming to stay in the hut on Crag Tower. The Dappella helped draw the possums.
text:

Poppy has never stayed away from home before, and her mum says she has been sleeping with the light on. Wren wants Poppy to feel safe and excited, not worried.

Hi Poppy! Thank you for your drawing. Don't worry, the hut isn't haunted, it's just full of possums. The scratching noises at night are just the possums having a midnight snack. One of them is called Biscuit, and he loves apple. If you're brave, you can feed him a slice. The hut has a big fireplace and a window where you can see the stars. I'll be right there with you, and we'll make hot chocolate with marshmallows. Bring your pyjamas with the penguins on them. Mo is cooking pancakes, but don't worry, I'll make sure they're normal ones. See you soon!
Love, Wren

frame: Ari wrote a recount for the class blog. The Stagglet is reading the last line twice.
text: Last Saturday, Mum took me snorkelling at Gull Bay for the very first time. I had never put my face under the sea before, and my stomach was in knots. First, Mum showed me how to spit in my mask so it wouldn't fog up, which was disgusting but worked. Then we waded in up to our waists, and I practised breathing through the snorkel while standing still. When I finally put my face in, I forgot to breathe at all, because a school of silver fish was flashing past my knees. Mum tapped my shoulder and pointed at a rock covered in purple sea urchins. Near the jetty, a huge blue groper swam right up to my mask and stared at me as if I was the strange one. By the time we came out, my fingers were wrinkly and my lips were salty, and I didn't want to leave. On the drive home, I fell asleep with my mask still on my head. That was the day the ocean stopped being scary and started being mine.

frame: Wren is finishing her report on wedge-tailed eagles. The Fittlet is perched on her pencil.
text: Wedge-tailed Eagles. Wedge-tailed eagles are the largest birds of prey in Australia, with wings that can stretch more than two metres from tip to tip. They are found all over the mainland and in Tasmania, from deserts and farmland to the high, snowy country around Scaffold Peaks. Adults are mostly dark brown, almost black, while young birds are a lighter, golden brown that darkens as they age. The eagle gets its name from its long tail, which is shaped like a wedge and helps it steer as it soars on warm, rising air. Like other birds of prey, they have hooked beaks for tearing meat and strong, curved claws called talons for gripping. Wedge-tailed eagles hunt rabbits, lizards and other small animals, and they also feed on animals that are already dead. Their eyesight is so sharp that they can spot a rabbit moving from more than a kilometre away. They can soar higher than almost any other Australian bird, sometimes more than a kilometre above the ground. Pairs often stay together for many years and return to the same nesting area each spring. A pair usually raises one or two chicks a year, and both parents take turns bringing food to the nest. Wren wants to add one more sentence. options: A, because it is true of every wedge-tailed eagle, not just one bird.

frame: Tully wrote about how she made the Reef Rays junior squad. The Ledgeling has heard it eleven times.
text: Every evening after school, Tully went down to the frozen oval at the bottom of Scaffold Peaks to practise kicking. Her goal was simple: to make the Reef Rays junior squad, the team she had supported since she was four years old. She set up a row of witches' hats along the boundary and tried to kick the ball between them from fifty metres out. Most of her kicks sailed wide, and one bounced off a seagull, who was not impressed. Her fingers went numb inside her gloves, and her breath came out in clouds. Still, she kept a notebook in her pocket and wrote down every single kick, the good ones and the terrible ones, until the floodlights switched off at seven. Six months later, on the same frozen oval, Tully kicked her hundredth goal in a row without missing once. The Reef Rays coach, who had been watching quietly from the fence, wrote something in a notebook of her own. Then she walked over and handed Tully an envelope with the club's logo on the front.

Which type you have depends on your family, a bit like the colour of your eyes. Gus says earwax is not dirt at all, but a clever piece of body engineering. text: Field report from Dr Imogen Hale, Southern Ocean survey. For six days our research vessel, the Albatross, has been anchored beside the ice shelf, waiting for the weather to clear. On the seventh morning, the fog finally lifted, and the crew spotted a southern right whale drifting near the bow. She was enormous, longer than the vessel's lifeboat, and her back was crusted with pale patches that looked like barnacles. Our team lowered a small underwater camera on a cable, hoping to film her feeding. For almost twenty minutes, she ignored the camera completely. Then, without warning, she rolled onto her side, opened one huge eye and swam straight towards it. She nudged it gently with her head, once, twice, three times, until the cable swung like a pendulum. The footage is wobbly, but it shows something remarkable. Pressed against her side, beneath one flipper, is a calf no bigger than a car. It had been hiding there for the whole visit, just out of view of our camera. We had no idea it was there. Within an hour the pair had vanished into the grey water, and the fog rolled back in.
